item.title: A common neural axis links image distinctiveness and memorability
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Utochkin, I., Chang, W., Vogel, E. K., Awh, E.
Stimulus-specific memorability, the tendency for people to remember and forget the same stimuli, is a powerful predictor of memory performance that is independent of the study and retrieval factors that have dominated memory research. Critically, memorability can be defined in two ways: "Hit-ability" (H-ability) and "false alarm-ability" (FA-ability), the probability of correctly recognizing studied items or falsely recognizing unstudied items, respectively. Although past work has suggested that these are dissociable facets of memorability, challenging single-factor explanations, we present neural and computational evidence that they share a common neural axis. The neural signature of high H-ability matched the signature for low FA-ability, showing that these parameters have inverse relationships with a common factor. Moreover, we show that image distinctiveness predicts the flipped relationship between H-ability and FA-ability in both behavior and neural activity, providing a unifying explanation of stimulus-specific memorability.

item.title: Learned associations constrain anticipatory visual dynamics and enhance sensory and motor readiness to facilitate perceptual decisions
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Zhang, L., Yuan, M., Zhang, H., Morris Moscovitch, M., Alain, C.
Learned cue target associations can guide attention to facilitate perceptual decision making, yet how they shape the content and dynamics of neural activity, and whether this facilitation reflects anticipatory preparation, post-target sensory enhancement, or both, remains unclear. Here, we used magnetoencephalography while participants made living/nonliving judgments about visual objects (e.g., cat/violin) with left- or right-hand button presses. Cue category associations were established through repeated pairings: predictive cues always preceded one target category, whereas uninformative cues preceded both categories equally often. Predictive cues facilitated behavioral responses despite limited explicit awareness of the learned associations. Representational similarity analysis showed that prediction preactivated target-specific representations in the visual cortex resembling target evoked activity before target onset. Prediction also elicited anticipatory, response specific motor beta suppression. Together, these findings supported anticipatory preparation, with little evidence of enhanced posttarget visual specificity. Posttarget visual specificity and anticipatory motor preparation independently predicted response speed, with hierarchical drift diffusion modeling linking greater visual specificity to faster evidence accumulation and stronger motor preparation to shorter nondecision time (a model parameter reflecting sensory encoding and motor execution). Beyond representational content, prediction also constrained the evolution of anticipatory visual population activity, and more constrained, stable early visual trajectories predicted faster responses. These population dynamics were associated with faster evidence accumulation, lower decision thresholds, and shorter non-decision time. Together, these findings suggest that associative memory facilitates perceptual decisions by shaping the content and dynamics of anticipatory neural activity, with partially dissociable contributions from visual processing and motor preparation.

item.title: How striatal neurons influence decision-making depends on broader circuit context: evidence from theory-driven cell type identification
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Yu, Z., Verstynen, T., Rubin, J.
Neural cell types are often conceived as having fixed computational roles, yet their behavioral contributions may depend on the broader circuit state. In the striatum, for example, direct and indirect pathway spiny projection neurons (SPNs) are typically described as facilitating or suppressing actions, respectively. However, emerging observations of striatal activity, such as modulation related to action timing, action vigor, and reactive inhibition, call this dichotomy into question. Here we develop a state-space framework linking striatal population activity to decision dynamics by combining a spiking cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic (CBGT) model with large-scale in vivo recordings from mice performing a two-choice task. Modeled activity patterns guided the inference of putative striatal SPN subtypes in the empirical recordings, enabling reconstruction of decision trajectories through an underlying state space. Across simulated and experimental data, these trajectories revealed a shared set of decision dynamics and identified three state-dependent roles of indirect pathway activity: preserving uncertainty when active alone, signifying choice commitment when coactive with the direct pathway in the same action channel, and slowing decisions when recruited in the opposing channel. To interpret these roles mechanistically, we mapped state transitions onto previously described basal ganglia control ensembles (responsiveness, pliancy, and choice) that translate circuit activity into the evidence accumulation process, and we found that each role was associated with a distinct pattern of control ensemble engagement that tunes decision policy. These analyses support a context-dependent view of SPN function, in which their moment-to-moment impact emerges from the evolving profile of dynamics throughout the CBGT circuit.

item.title: Same Movements, Different Skills: How Context Shapes Learning in Humans and Neural Networks
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Gupta, M. W., Taylor, J. A.
What determines whether experiences are integrated into shared representations or split? Motor skill learning offers a revealing test: when two tasks require an identical sequence of movements, both intuition and theory suggest that practice in one should generalize to the other. Yet we find that changing context can make identical movements different skills. In simple recurrent networks trained on the same sequence across contexts, splitting was greatest when strong contextual inputs coincided with a high initial weight scale; neither alone sufficed. Greater representational separation coincided with separate context-specific learning curves. Humans practicing the same finger sequence while alternating between two performance-irrelevant contexts likewise exhibited context-specific curves, rather than the single continuous trajectory observed when practicing in a single context. State-space modeling favored split learning states in humans and very weakly coupled states in the most context-dependent networks. These findings have broader implications for understanding how learning generalizes across contexts.

item.title: Sentence-level neural dynamics in speech motor cortex
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Levi-Aharoni, H., Jude, J. J., Haro, S., Acosta, A. J., Allcroft, S. B., Ottenhoff, M. C., Card, N. S., Wairagkar, M., Iacobacci, C., Pritchard, A. L., Richards, B., Brandman, D. M., Stavisky, S. D., Au Yong, N., Pandarinath, C., Paulk, A. C., Hadar, P. N., Li, J., Williams, Z. M., Cash, S. S., Simeral, J. D., Hochberg, L. R., Rubin, D. B.
Prior recordings from speech motor cortex have revealed phonemic, syllabic, articulatory and speech-sequence representations, while more recent studies indicate that activity may also reflect higher-order features of speech production. However, whether speech motor cortex is sensitive to the linguistic organization of sentences remains unclear. Here we show that single-unit activity in speech motor cortex contains information about sentence-level linguistic structure. In three BrainGate2 participants with implanted microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, we recorded neural activity during an instructed-delay speech task comprising English sentences, word lists, syntactically structured nonword sentences and nonword lists. Neural activity in areas 6v and 55b contained speech- and language-related components, with stronger stimulus-condition effects in 55b, and stimulus condition was decodable in all three participants. In two larger datasets, semantic categories of English sentences were decodable from neural activity. These findings demonstrate that speech motor cortex encodes information about linguistic structure and semantic content at the level of sentences.

item.title: Beyond Cortical Scaffolding: Functional Network Specialization in Reading Development
Retrospective lexical cues enhance access to uncued sensory features of past auditory words
Picture this Scent
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: SocArXiv
Oriente Pimentel Aldaz et al.
This study investigates how olfactory perception is represented across multiple behavioural measures, including visual mental imagery, colour correspondences, odour familiarity, odour identification, and perceptual similarity. It examines whether these different responses converge on a shared representational organisation of scent, with a particular focus on source-centred visual imagery and crossmodal associations.
